players.product: Automated test equipment (UltraFLEXplus, Photon 100 SiPho/CPO test, Omnyx board test) for AI compute

quarterly_data.signal: Q4 2025 results (CEO Greg Smith; CFO Michelle Turner, on her first Teradyne call): fourth quarter sales were $1.083 billion with non-GAAP EPS of $1.80, both above the high end of guidance, on 41% sequential revenue growth and more than 100% non-GAAP earnings growth. It was the highest revenue quarter of 2025 and the second highest in company history, 'only $3 million below our record during the mobile boom of 2021.' Semi Test revenue was $883 million, 'fueled by AI compute and memory demand', with SoC revenue $647 million, up 47% quarter-on-quarter; Product Test was $110 million on defense and aerospace demand; Robotics was $89 million, up 19% from Q3. Non-GAAP gross margin was 57.2% (including an inventory write-down on legacy products), non-GAAP operating profit roughly doubled to $314 million (a 29% operating rate) and free cash flow was $219 million. Full year 2025: revenue $3.2 billion, up 13%; the Semiconductor Test Group grew 19%, with SoC test revenue up 23% 'driven mainly by networking and VIP compute'; compute became the largest component of company revenue and grew 90% year-over-year; Semi Test is now close to 80% of sales (up from the low 70s); gross margin 58.3%; non-GAAP EPS $3.96 (up 23%); free cash flow $450 million.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 sales $1.083 billion; non-GAAP EPS $1.80; 41% sequential revenue growth; Semi Test $883 million; SoC $647 million, up 47%; full-year revenue $3.2 billion, up 13%; compute grew 90%; non-GAAP EPS $3.96

quarterly_data.signal: AI SHARE OF REVENUE AND THE Q1 2026 GUIDE: AI demand drove 40% to 50% of revenue in Q3 2025, more than 60% in Q4, and upwards of 70% is expected in Q1 2026. Beyond compute and memory, the cloud and edge AI build-out is also driving demand for power management, SLT, HDD, ICT and optical test. Q1 2026 sales are guided to $1.15 billion to $1.25 billion, a new quarterly record 'driven by all things AI' (the midpoint is 11% growth from Q4 and 75% from Q1 2025), with non-GAAP EPS of $1.89 to $2.25 on 158 million diluted shares, gross margin of 58.5% to 59.5%, OpEx up 6% (26% to 28% of sales) and a 32% operating profit rate at the midpoint. Shape of 2026: 2025 sales were 40% first half / 60% second half, and 2026 is expected to be the inverse, with roughly 60% of sales in the first half, because 'major programs that we're a part of are first half loaded.' The CFO said 'we are entering the year with a healthy backlog' that gives better first-half insight than the usual 13 weeks of demand visibility. She cautioned against assuming linear quarters and gave no Q2 guide. The CEO added: 'We don't have great visibility into the second half.' and 'We expect that we're in kind of a 2-, 3-quarter surge that may lead to a shorter period of digestion afterwards.' The 2026 ATE TAM is described as robust growth, 'like 20% to 40% growth for the year, but we don't know where in that range it would land'. Management said it is not signalling the 30% midpoint, and agreed that the SoC TAM should grow faster than the memory TAM.
quarterly_data.figure: Q1 2026 sales $1.15 billion to $1.25 billion (record); non-GAAP EPS $1.89 to $2.25; AI upwards of 70% of Q1 revenue (more than 60% in Q4); roughly 60% of 2026 sales in the first half; 2026 ATE TAM 20% to 40% growth range

quarterly_data.signal: NEW EVERGREEN TARGET EARNINGS MODEL, anchored to TAM size rather than a calendar year: management sees the ATE TAM reaching $12 billion to $14 billion, up from about $9 billion in 2025, which it believes is achievable within the midterm. At that TAM Teradyne targets roughly $6 billion of revenue ('nearly 2x 2025's revenue and 2.5x the earnings per share'), with gross margin of 59% to 61%, OpEx of 27% to 29%, operating profit of 30% to 34% and non-GAAP EPS of $9.50 to $11. Growth is expected to be proportional across the groups (roughly 80-10-10), with Semi Test growing faster than the ATE market through share gains; the CEO put Teradyne 'in the low 40s' of ATE share in that model (IST sits outside the ATE TAM). Assumptions: compute share gains from a relatively low base; the mobile TAM recovering on device complexity rather than units to about halfway between today and the prior peak (about 1.5x today), with mobile fleet reuse moderating capacity adds; auto/industrial growth tied to Edge AI, EVs and 800-volt data center power, where the power group acquired from Infineon last year covers the wide-bandgap power market. On captive testers, one big SoC player and one big memory player run captive ATE strategies; the SoC one is expected to change over the next couple of years 'as there are a broader range of customers for foundry that want commercial platforms.' The pace depends on data-center silicon growth: 'from '24 to '25, it's like 60% more silicon revenue in data centers. Looking out to 2026, it's way more than 100% year-on-year growth.'
quarterly_data.figure: ATE TAM $12 billion to $14 billion (from about $9 billion in 2025); roughly $6 billion revenue; gross margin 59% to 61%; operating profit 30% to 34%; non-GAAP EPS $9.50 to $11

quarterly_data.signal: SoC TEST MARKET AND MIX: the 2025 SoC TAM reached a record, nearly 60% larger than 2024. The CEO's breakdown, subject to final third-party totals: compute 'in the neighborhood of $5 billion', mobility about $1 billion, auto/industrial just under $1 billion and service in the $700 million range. The VIP (custom ASIC) portion of compute is 'just over $600' (unit not spoken). Teradyne's SoC product revenue mix moved from about 10% compute / 50% auto-industrial / 40% mobile in 2023 to nearly 50% compute in 2025, with auto/industrial and mobile about a quarter each. Networking grew on the high density of network connections in AI data centers. For 2026, compute is expected to grow significantly from a very high base, auto/industrial to recover moderately and mobile is uncertain (unit volume, mix, capital efficiency); Teradyne expects to gain share 'in the single digits in SoC test'. Customer concentration: the three 10% customers in 2025 were two specifying customers ('one was in the mobile space, one was in the compute space') and one purchasing customer that 'does it all'; asked about size, the CFO said 'Roughly 10%. It's not substantially higher than that.'
quarterly_data.figure: 2025 SoC TAM nearly 60% larger than 2024; compute in the neighborhood of $5 billion; mobility about $1 billion; service $700 million range; SoC revenue nearly 50% compute (about 10% in 2023)

quarterly_data.signal: VIP (CUSTOM AI ASIC) COMPUTE TEST: Teradyne believes it held about 50% share of VIP compute in 2025, in a segment where only a few players drive large ATE purchases, which made 2025 revenue lumpy. The CEO said 'no share is safe. We are challenging for sockets that we don't have. We're being challenged for sockets that we do have.' He is cautious about sizing ASIC programs not yet in volume because hyperscalers benchmark their own chips against commercial parts and 'will only take their ASICs to full volume if they see an advantage in like tokens per watt'. Long term Teradyne expects to hold about 50%, though the figure will be noisy quarter to quarter and year to year. In a $12 billion to $14 billion TAM it expects to add VIP logos, but 'It's more like 4 or 5 different programs.' He sees a steady state where 'Teradyne and Advantest are going to be competing on a generational basis for new design wins', decided on tester features and reliability more than incumbency.
quarterly_data.figure: about 50% VIP compute share in 2025; 4 or 5 different programs in a $12 billion to $14 billion TAM

quarterly_data.signal: MERCHANT GPU SECOND SOURCE, BEFORE QUALIFICATION: Teradyne is 'making great project -- progress' toward production qualification on merchant GPU test. The process is very complex and very expensive and the release date is hard to pin down, but the CEO is 'really confident'. Q1 2026 guidance includes NO merchant GPU revenue; it is 'more of a factor in the second half of 2026', and 'a significant ramp associated with merchant GPU would have an impact in the second half.' He expects it to be 'a material amount of revenue for us, but it would not be a heck of a lot of share inside of the account where we won', starting at single-digit share. In dual-source accounts vendors eventually balance between 30% and 70% share; 30% is not a ceiling, but it will take time to get there. The $6 billion model includes merchant GPU, but 'we don't assume a radically high share in the merchant GPU space.' Why customers pick Teradyne: a more resilient supply chain with generally shorter lead times; better production reliability and uptime, with OSATs advocating for the tester; a next-generation instrument set now in beta test that 'will significantly increase the amount of power available to the devices and very importantly, the amount of memory for the test programs and the test patterns that these devices are going to need'; and mission-mode test, 'almost like building a server into the tester itself'. New test insertions and more specialized chiplets per merchant GPU device give 'more shots on goal' and grow the compute TAM.
quarterly_data.figure: no merchant GPU revenue in Q1 guidance; more of a factor in the second half of 2026; single-digit share to start; dual-source vendors balanced between 30% and 70% share

quarterly_data.signal: WAFER-TO-DATA-CENTER TEST (Product Test Group): Product Test revenue grew 8% in 2025 on defense and aerospace, and all of its business lines are expected to grow in 2026. Quantifi Photonics has been integrated into the group, with the LitePoint and Production Board Test sales teams trained on the Quantifi line. Production Board Test 'tests the server trays that devices go into', and Quantifi Photonics instruments 'test silicon photonics from device to rack'; the CEO cited a 'leadership position in silicon photonics device test'. Teradyne announced a joint venture with MultiLane, 'a global leader in high-speed I/O and data center interconnect test solutions'. The JV, MultiLane Test Products, is being formed 'to serve the growing AI data center demand'. Teradyne will be the majority owner and MultiLane keeps a minority position; closing is expected in Q2 '26. Results will be consolidated into Product Test with a new noncontrolling-interest line, and the deal is expected to be 'accretive in 2026 with a de minimis impact to EPS.' Midterm Product Test growth is tied to 'compute, Defense, Photonics, high-speed Internet data and data centers.'
quarterly_data.figure: Product Test grew 8% in 2025; MultiLane JV close expected in Q2 '26 with Teradyne as majority owner; accretive in 2026 with de minimis EPS impact

quarterly_data.signal: RECORD MEMORY TEST QUARTER, AND DRAM/HBM NOW DOMINATE THE TAM: Q4 2025 memory revenue was $206 million, up 61% quarter-on-quarter and a record sales quarter for the memory business. In 2025 memory test revenue was up slightly in a roughly flat market 'on continued share gains in HBM and DRAM final test'. The overall memory test TAM was down about 4% from 2024, and Teradyne gained a little share; 'A bright spot' was AI compute demand for both HBM and DRAM. The CEO put the 2025 memory TAM at just under $1.4 billion, of which $1.2 billion was DRAM and the rest FLASH. In 2020-2021 the memory test market was split more or less evenly between FLASH and DRAM; in 2025 DRAM and HBM made up nearly 90% of it. Years ago Teradyne was absent from several parts of the memory market; 'Now we feel like we are in most of the segments for most of the customers.'
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 memory revenue $206 million, up 61% (record); 2025 memory TAM down about 4%, just under $1.4 billion ($1.2 billion DRAM); DRAM and HBM nearly 90% of the memory TAM

quarterly_data.signal: 2026 MEMORY TEST OUTLOOK: the CEO said 'we expect a resurgent memory market in 2026 with low double-digit TAM growth over 2025, driven by continued strength in HBM and DRAM, and we expect to continue our incremental share gains', and expects the DRAM/HBM-heavy mix to continue into 2026. Over the midterm the memory TAM should grow 'more incrementally' than compute, and Teradyne can 'split the share and ride the trends' now that it serves most segments. One big memory player runs a captive ATE strategy, which the CEO thinks is 'probably more persistent' than the captive SoC one.
quarterly_data.figure: 2026 memory test TAM: low double-digit growth over 2025, driven by HBM and DRAM

quarterly_data.signal: INTEGRATED SYSTEM TEST (HDD/SLT) WIDENS ITS BASE: IST revenue grew over 50% from 2024 to 2025. Through 2024 it served the HDD and mobile SLT markets, mostly through one large customer in each. A new mobile SLT customer won in 2024 ramped strongly in 2025; in 2025 Teradyne entered compute SLT and won 2 customers; and in late 2025 it received orders from a new HDD customer, ramping in 2026. The CEO described the HDD win as commercial test 'complementing internal test' and 'a way for a customer to effectively build capacity', and said HDD revenue is 'going to like double between 2025 and 2026'. The midterm model also counts on IST growth from compute SLT and HDD wins.
quarterly_data.figure: IST over 50% growth from 2024 to 2025; HDD test revenue to double between 2025 and 2026; 2 compute SLT customers won in 2025
